est l’alphabet utilisé pour écrire le co: is the alphabet used to write Korean. Its letters represent sounds. They are grouped into small blocks: each block corresponds to a syllable.
나무, formé de deux syllabes 나 + 무, signif: 나무, made of two syllables 나 + 무, means “tree”.
Une consonne est un son pour lequel la b: A consonant is a sound where the mouth slows down or blocks the air, like n or m. A vowel is a sound you can let ring out without that blocking, like a or i. A syllable contains a vowel, possibly with consonants around it.

Les lettres ne sont pas des mots à tradu: Letters are not words to translate: ㄴ does not mean “tree”. It is their combination in 나무 that forms this word.
2. Les voyelles : le cœur du son: 2. Vowels: the heart of the sound
Commence par ces six voyelles. Les repèr: Start with these six vowels. The English hints and the romanisation are approximate: above all, listen to the examples.
a : ouvre la bouche, sans arrondir les l: a: open your mouth, without rounding your lips.
eo : une seule voyelle, plus ouverte que: eo: a single vowel, more open than ㅗ; don’t read it “ay-o”.
u dans la romanisation : proche du « ou: u in the romanisation: close to “oo” in “food”.
eu : une seule voyelle, langue en arrièr: eu: a single vowel, tongue pulled back and lips unrounded; there is no exact English equivalent.
Un deuxième petit trait ajoute un son in: A second small stroke adds an initial sound close to “y”: ㅏ → ㅑ (ya), ㅓ → ㅕ (yeo), ㅗ → ㅛ (yo), ㅜ → ㅠ (yu).
Pourquoi écrit-on 아 et pas seulement ㅏ ?: Why write 아 and not just ㅏ?
Un bloc syllabique commence par une plac: A syllable block starts with a consonant slot. When the sound starts directly with a vowel, ㅇ goes in that slot: at the start of the block, it is silent. So 아 is read a.
À essayer sans quiz : écoute 아 puis 우. R: To try without a quiz: listen to 아 then 우. Copy each block five times while saying the sound, then compare 어 and 오.
3. Les consonnes : commencer et fermer u: 3. Consonants: starting and closing a sound
. Avec ㅏ, elles deviennent 나, 마, 사, 하. L: . With ㅏ, they become 나, 마, 사, 하. The letter ㄴ is called 니은, but in 나 it represents the sound n: the name of a letter and its sound are two different things.
ㄱ, ㄷ et ㅂ ne correspondent pas exactemen: ㄱ, ㄷ and ㅂ do not match exactly one English letter: depending on their position and surroundings, they can sound like g/k, d/t and b/p. ㄹ can sound like a quick tap of the tongue between vowels, and like an l at the end.
opposent des consonnes simples, aspirées: contrast plain, aspirated and tense consonants. Aspirated ones let more air through; tense ones need a tighter articulation. It is not simply speaking louder.
muet au début de 아, mais un son « ng » à: silent at the start of 아, but an “ng” sound at the end of 강. So you have to look at its place in the block.
À essayer : lis 나 → 누 → 니. La consonne r: To try: read 나 → 누 → 니. The consonant stays the same; only the vowel changes.

A vertical vowel goes on the right.
La voyelle horizontale se place sous la: A horizontal vowel goes under the consonant.
The final consonant goes at the very bottom.
La finale ferme le bloc : on n’ajoute pa: The final consonant closes the block: no vowel is added after it.
La consonne du bas s’appelle le: The bottom consonant is called the
. Dans 한, c’est ㄴ. Dans 나, il n’y en a p: . In 한, it is ㄴ. In 나, there is none. A syllable can also have two written final consonants; their pronunciation is practised later depending on the word and the next sound.
Pour écrire, organise les traits du haut: To write, arrange the strokes from top to bottom and from left to right inside the block. Keep each syllable inside an imaginary square. Copy 한, then 국, then 한국: this last word has two syllables.

한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ ; 국 = ㄱ + ㅜ + ㄱ. Deux bloc: 한 = ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ; 국 = ㄱ + ㅜ + ㄱ. Two blocks with final consonants.
